title: Two HD 93683 fits require companions above 0.09 solar masses under exact Newtonian force and stated orbit bounds
abstract: We prove a companion mass bound from a finite change of orbital plane in an isolated Newtonian triple. The force is exact. No orbit averaging, fixed outer eccentricity, or constant outer angular momentum magnitude is used. The proof combines a finite-separation torque inequality, a bound on outer relative speed, and a new finite-interval angular momentum inequality. If |L2|^6 |dL2/dt| <= B, its endpoint chord d obeys d^7 <= 448 B T. Two published HD 93683 point fits then require companion masses of at least 0.09196 and 0.09333 solar masses. These values assume inner masses of 18 and 15 solar masses, a stated inner size envelope, endpoint eccentricities no larger than the fitted values, a larger inner barycentric radius below 0.1 of the outer separation, and nonpositive outer osculating Kepler energy throughout the interval. Inner eccentricity can change freely between endpoints while the inner orbit stays bound. Both photometric inclination branches and all nodes are allowed. A one-degree error at each endpoint lowers the first floor to 0.06834 solar masses. We give the proof, sensitivity results, 200,000 exact-force checks, 10,000 vector-path checks and five resolved synthetic triples. These are conditional necessary bounds, not measured masses, confidence limits, new detections or fits to new observations. The analysis does not show that an orbit can attain the floor or that the orbit envelopes hold in HD 93683.

display.caption: Conditional companion mass floors for two HD 93683 point fits. The left panel varies the allowed error of each endpoint normal. The right panel varies the separation ratio and outer speed cap. The curves are sensitivity scenarios, not confidence intervals.

The angular momentum inequality. The left panel shows scalar controls, not orbit fits. The right panel compares the allowed chord with the chord required by each point fit. Passing the condition does not establish an orbit.
Five resolved synthetic Newtonian triples test the local inequality. The examples include high inner and outer eccentricity. They are numerical checks, not fits to HD 93683.
